presentation.ear_right: Inside: violence in half of school classes, a ban on prosecutors' religious symbols, Tennessee halts executions

coverage.note: Built from headlines, RSS descriptions and the Ritzau copy carried in Kristeligt Dagblad's feed, published between 05:30 on Tuesday and 05:30 on Friday Copenhagen time, from 132 feeds at seventeen publishers. Three Financial Times feeds (Life & Arts, Opinion, Work & Careers) failed; the rest polled successfully. Danish outlets decide what is news; international titles are linked where they cover the same story. Nothing else was read.

copy.headline: Defence Command admits soldiers fired as passenger plane crossed Borris

extended.text: The Defence Command admitted on Thursday evening that soldiers fired 43 shots at Borris firing range in September 2025 while a Norwegian passenger plane was flying over it. It had previously said the shots came after the plane had passed. It maintains that the soldiers fired at drones in a different direction and that their ammunition could not reach the plane.

The shots are now placed between 20:06 and 20:08, based on a video recorded at 20:06 and a TDC record of a call at 20:07:57. The November 2025 report gave 20:20, although the Army Command had put the shots in the earlier window before that report; the new report does not say why.
'We made a mistake there, and I take responsibility for it,' said Peter Boysen, the army chief.
Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, told TV 2 News that the claim about drones had been substantiated.

standard.text: The Defence Command admitted on Thursday evening that soldiers fired 43 shots at Borris firing range in September 2025 while a Norwegian passenger plane was flying over it. It had previously said the shots came after the plane had passed. It maintains that the soldiers were firing at drones and could not have hit the plane.
The shots are now placed between 20:06 and 20:08, not at 20:20 as the November 2025 report stated. 'We made a mistake there, and I take responsibility for it,' said Peter Boysen, the army chief.

short.text: The Defence Command admitted on Thursday that soldiers fired 43 shots at Borris in September 2025 while a passenger plane was overhead. It maintains that they were firing at drones, not at the plane.

copy.headline_short: Army admits Borris shots coincided with plane
copy.deck: The army chief takes the blame for a wrong timeline but insists his soldiers were firing at drones.

copy.headline: Violence reaches half of school classes as government readies bill for teachers

standard.text: More than half of Danish school classes saw violence between pupils during a school year, according to a report by Epinion and Als Research for the education ministry, and the government will soon table a bill giving teachers more scope to intervene physically.
Three quarters of the youngest classes (kindergarten class to third grade) were affected, and the problems are also marked in classes with support needs.
Most of the violence happens outside lessons when play, sport or jokes get out of hand, and only 7 per cent of cases are deliberate and planned.
Magnus Heunicke, the education minister, also wants to be able to remove pupils from the class.

short.text: More than half of Danish school classes saw violence between pupils during a school year, a report for the education ministry finds, and the government will soon table a bill giving teachers more scope to intervene physically.

copy.headline_short: Violence reaches half of school classes
copy.deck: Three in four of the youngest classes have seen it, and the minister promises teachers more power to step in.

callouts.text: The extent of violence in the public schools is, to put it mildly, worrying.

copy.headline: Justice minister moves to ban religious symbols for prosecutors

standard.text: Prosecutors should face the same ban on religious and political symbols in court that has applied to judges since 2009, Nicolai Wammen, the justice minister, wrote on Thursday in a reply to Ekstra Bladet.
Berlingske reports that a majority for barring prosecutors from wearing headscarves in court is forming in the Folketing, but that the governing parties are split.
The debate began when Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor in Viborg, wrote on LinkedIn that she was proud to be Denmark's first prosecutor to wear a headscarf.
The Association of Public Prosecutors tells DR it backs her unconditionally and that she has fully complied with the current rules.

short.text: Nicolai Wammen, the justice minister, wants prosecutors barred from wearing religious and political symbols in court, as judges have been since 2009.

copy.headline_short: Minister wants prosecutors' religious symbols banned
copy.deck: One prosecutor's headscarf has split the government, while a majority for a ban takes shape in the Folketing.

callouts.text: Neither Muslim nor other visible religious symbols must be able to weaken citizens' trust that what takes place in Danish courtrooms is objective.

copy.headline: Tennessee halts executions after condemned woman survives lethal injection

standard.text: Christa Pike is in critical condition and receiving life-saving treatment after surviving two injections meant to kill her at a Nashville prison on Wednesday evening, her lawyer says, according to the New York Times.
Bill Lee, Tennessee's governor, has ordered an independent inquiry and halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Her lawyers have asked him to commute her sentence to life imprisonment, and Randy Spivey, one of them, calls the situation 'cruel and agonising', according to the New York Times.
The state's protocol prescribes a second set of injections if the first fails, but says nothing of what follows if the second fails too.

short.text: Christa Pike is in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections in Tennessee on Wednesday, and Bill Lee, the state's governor, has ordered an independent inquiry and halted executions for the rest of the year.

copy.headline_short: Tennessee halts executions after failed injection

copy.headline: EU clears the way for return centres outside Europe

standard.text: EU countries on Thursday adopted the return regulation, which for the first time makes it lawful for member states to set up return centres outside the EU. Only Spain voted against, and because the European Parliament has already backed the regulation, it can soon take effect.

Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece want agreements with countries outside the EU so that rejected asylum seekers can be sent there next year. Morten Bødskov, the immigration minister, hopes the first agreement can be reached before the end of this year.
Chiara Catelli of PICUM, an organisation that opposes the centres, said the regulation gives member states 'a free hand to send people to places they do not even know'.

short.text: EU countries on Thursday adopted a regulation that for the first time makes it lawful to set up return centres outside the EU; Morten Bødskov, the immigration minister, hopes the first agreement can be reached before the end of the year.

copy.deck: Only Spain voted no, and Denmark and four allies are now looking for countries willing to take rejected asylum seekers.
